validator: draft 1 passed with no hard or soft problems; the faults below are the critic's
keep: The idea is named up front: a net force changes how a thing moves rather than keeping it moving. The rest of the lesson builds the graph tools, then the three laws and momentum, each from the last.

The speed-time graph is a recall from Calculus fundamentals by name, not re-taught. The four steady-acceleration equations are each read off the slope or the area, with u, v, a, t and s named, and one worked case (0.5 to 1 m/s over 2 s, 1.5 m) checked both ways.
The misconception is shown failing: the trolley that stops when you let go is stopped by friction, and with friction off it rolls on. Screen 5 puts both sides of the rule on the picture.
The brief's example figures are kept and computed: 2000 kg from 0 to 0.5 m/s in 2 s needs 500 N net, with the drive's 600 N and the brake's 400 N worked from an example 100 N of friction.

Fourteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with three mixed puzzles (12, 13, 14). Each brief misconception has its own wrong pick: motion needs a force (6), the push instead of the net force (8), slope and area swapped (2, 4), moment for momentum (10, 600 N m), the third law pair forgotten (12, none and 500 N), and momentum mistaken for a force (14, 1200 N).

Conservation of momentum is derived, not asserted: equal and opposite pushes for the same time move equal and opposite amounts of momentum. Only the third law itself, which has no source in the research, is stated as a textbook rule.
The analogy is the one Differential equations set up, mass as inductance, and it reproduces the main result: a voltage sets how fast a current changes, not the current.
fix: False absolute: the opening 'A force does not keep a thing moving' is untrue on any real rail, where the drive keeps the trolley moving against friction. Say a moving thing needs no NET force to keep moving.

False absolute: the rule of thumb 'steady speed means zero net force, whatever the speed' fails for a body turning at a steady speed. Say steady speed in a straight line, and say the rail is straight wherever the explanation leans on it.
Causal step skipped: 'F × t = m × the change in speed' holds as written only for a steady net force. Say so, and say why a newton second is the same unit as a kg m/s (a newton is a kg m/s²).
Causal step skipped: 'speeds it up, slows it down or turns it' gives turning no reason. Say a velocity has a direction too, so changing direction is also a change of velocity.
Talks about instead of teaching: 'This lesson treats each trolley as one solid body' names the teaching model but not what real cases lose. Add one closing sentence: wheel spin, slope and air drag.
Ambiguity: 'Take t out of those two' does not say which two. Say the first two, v = u + at and s = ½(u + v)t.
One letter, two meanings: the analogy writes v = L di/dt with v as a voltage, in a lesson where v is the end speed. Write it in words.

Footnote over-reach: [^4] sits on a takeaway about net force ÷ mass, which its quote ('a change in velocity means acceleration') does not cover. Move [^4] to the sentence it supports and leave the takeaway, a summary of the steps above, unfootnoted.
The first-law sentence 'with no friction, nothing would slow it' leaves out air drag. Add it, and add air drag to ignores as what a curious reader may think the picture forgets.
Ignores: 'the area under it is the same' gives no reason. Say the momentum the push moves sets the area, so the shared speed is the same.
Phone: the three readouts must wrap at 360 px (RUNBOOK 5). Say so in whatAmILookingAt so the build carries it.
research: Thin by necessity: only the first and second laws are sourced. The third law appears once as 'Textbooks add', and momentum, impulse and the four equations are derived from F = ma and the graph's slope and area, so nothing unsourced is dressed up as cited.
verdict: rewrite as draft 2 with the fixes above; no fault left needs a third draft if these land
